briefs.summary: On November 9, Exxon signed a first, non-binding agreement with Venezuela's state oil company to study oil projects there. Last quarter Exxon's sales were $113.16 billion, up 32.7% from a year earlier, and its profit per share rose to $4.23 from $1.88. Someone who put $1,000 into Exxon a year ago would have about $1,432 as of November 13.
bull: Profit per share jumped to $4.23 last quarter from $1.88 a year earlier, because oil prices are still far above where they were a year ago.
Exxon's refining business, which turns crude into gasoline and diesel, grew profit 181% to $11.4 billion through September 30, so it earns money even when crude prices fall.
Exxon aims to make a profit even if oil drops to $35 a barrel by 2027, far below today's $92, which gives it room if prices keep sliding.
bear: Brent oil fell to about $92 a barrel on November 16 after trading as high as $120 during the Iran conflict, and lower oil means less profit per barrel.
The Venezuela deal does not commit Exxon to any project, and Exxon still needs a real contract and stable rules before it would invest.
The stock lost 4.7% in a month, more than the S&P 500's 3.1%, and sits about 11% below its 52-week high of $188.50.

briefs.summary: On November 16, J&J agreed to buy Ollin Biosciences for $2.2 billion in cash plus up to about $1.13 billion more if goals are met, with the deal expected to close before the end of 2026. Ollin's main drug, OLN324, is in its final stage of testing for wet AMD and diabetic eye swelling, two causes of vision loss. Blackstone will pay J&J $750 million over several years to fund that testing, in return for a small cut of future sales. Earlier, the FDA approved Rybrevant Faspro for head and neck cancer on November 5, and Caplyta passed a second final-stage bipolar test on November 10.
bull: Tremfya, an immune drug, grew sales 68% to $2.40 billion last quarter, and the CEO says it can become a $10 billion-a-year drug.
Blackstone pays $750 million toward Ollin's final testing, so J&J takes on less of the cost and risk of the new eye drug.
A new psoriatic arthritis pill, Icotyde, helped 58% of patients in a final-stage test on November 7, adding another possible big seller.
bear: At 42.8 times its past-year profit, J&J costs about twice as much as the average S&P 500 stock, so bad news could hit the price hard.
Products with $4 to $4.5 billion in yearly sales lose patent protection in 2027, which lets cheaper copies take sales away.
The stock trades above analysts' average price goal of about $279, and two recent deals cut 2026 profit per share by $0.64.

briefs.about: The Dow Jones Industrial Average tracks 30 large, well-known US companies, like Apple, Walmart and Coca-Cola. It is one of the oldest stock market measures, started in 1896.
briefs.whyMoved: The Dow fell 1.64%, or 848 points, on Tuesday to 50,759.42, a bigger drop than the S&P 500 or Nasdaq; it was at 53,356 on November 4, so it has lost about 4.9% in two weeks. Salesforce, a Dow member, was its worst stock, down 9.45% to $194.52, and UnitedHealth fell 5.42%. Because the Dow holds only 30 companies, a big drop in one or two of them pulls the whole average down much harder than in the 500-company S&P 500. Home Depot fell 2.45%, Microsoft 2.27% and Disney 1.48%, so the selling hit old, well-known companies more than chip makers.

bull: Retail sales beat forecasts at 0.2% in October, and smaller companies earn most of their money inside the US, so steady shoppers help them.

briefs.about: The Russell 2000 tracks about 2,000 smaller US companies. It shows how smaller businesses, which often depend more on loans and the US economy, are doing.
briefs.whyMoved: The Russell 2000 fell 1.50% on Tuesday to 2,701.87, more than the S&P 500's 1.03% drop; it was 2,857 on November 4, so smaller companies have lost about 5.4% in two weeks. Traders now see a 96.7% chance the Fed raises interest rates on December 9, and Fed officials said more hikes may come before spring 2027. Smaller companies borrow more of their money, often at rates that change, so higher rates eat directly into their profits. Builder confidence also fell to 25, the lowest since April 2012, which hurts the many small home and building companies in the index.

briefs.headline: Micron drops about 6% Monday on a new US chip export rule and Nvidia worries
briefs.about: Micron makes memory chips, the parts that store data in computers, phones and the giant data centers that run AI. Its main products are DRAM and NAND flash memory, plus HBM, a fast memory built for AI chips.
briefs.summary: Micron is now about 40% below its 52-week high of $1,255. Business is still booming: last quarter Micron's sales were $54.2 billion and it kept 87 cents of each sales dollar as gross profit, and it expects about $61.5 billion of sales this quarter. On November 14, a judge let a lawsuit go forward that says Micron, Samsung and SK Hynix worked together to keep memory prices high. A November 6 report said Nvidia asked TSMC to look into making memory chips, though Jefferies thinks real competition might not come until 2035.
bull: More than 75% of Micron's 2027 chips are already promised to customers, mostly at higher prices than 2026, so sales are largely locked in.
The stock costs only about 10 times its past-year profit, very cheap compared with most chip stocks, because it has fallen so far.
The average expert price goal of about $1,562 from 49 analysts is roughly double the current price.
bear: The new US export rule could cut chip sales into Asia and Brazil, and memory is one of the parts the US wants to watch.
A judge let a price-fixing lawsuit against Micron move ahead on November 14, which could mean costly penalties.
Micron's new Idaho factory will not make chips until mid-2027, so it cannot grow supply much if prices stay high.
briefs.nextEvent: Nvidia, Micron's biggest AI customer, reports results on November 17, 2026; Micron reports around December 16

briefs.name: Micron Technology
briefs.whyMoved: Micron fell about 6% on November 16, trading near $730 at midday after closing at $778.31 on November 13, its third drop in a row. Reports said the US government is adding a new rule that limits AI chips and computing going to China and makes buyers in places like Singapore, Malaysia and Brazil get export licenses, which could mean fewer memory chips sold. Investors also worry that Nvidia, the biggest buyer of Micron's AI memory, could slow orders after CEO Jensen Huang resigned. Almost all of Micron's huge profit now comes from selling memory for AI data centers, so any sign that AI chip buying slows hits the stock hard.

watch.what: Nvidia reports results after the close. Strong AI chip sales and a confident new leader would ease fears about memory orders; a weak outlook could push Micron lower.
Micron's expected quarterly report (estimated date). Good: sales near or above $61.5 billion. Bad: a lower forecast or falling memory prices.

market.why: On Tuesday, November 17, stocks fell for a fourth day in a row, and the S&P 500 had its lowest close since July. Software companies dropped hard, led by Salesforce (down 9.5%, the Dow's worst stock), and UnitedHealth fell 5.4%, so the Dow lost 848 points. Smaller Russell 2000 companies slid as traders now see about a 97% chance the Fed raises interest rates on December 9, making loans cost more, while chip stocks rose a bit, so the Nasdaq fell least.
